title: Hot/Cold Bridge and Slab Resilience for Paged KV under Continuous Batching
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem statement: As continuous batching increases throughput, the KV cache on GPU memory experiences high fragmentation and oscillating residency pressure that causes frequent host/GPU page swaps. Current slab allocation favors single-block lifetime decisions which leads to poor compaction opportunities and tail-latency spikes during sudden workload hotset shifts (multi-tenant inference bursts).

Goal: Design and implement a "Hot/Cold Bridge" layer and a slab-resilience policy for the paged KV cache so that: 1) hot tokens remain resident with minimal latency impact; 2) cold objects are drained/prefetched cooperatively with the batching runtime; 3) fragmentation is reduced with online micro-compaction without blocking streaming token generation. The solution must be safe for multi-model co-residency, require no infra-level reboots, and be compatible with our fallback routing rules for capacity tiers.
acceptance_criteria:
1) 95th token-latency during 1000 concurrent streams reduces by >= 20% under the 'hotset shift' synthetic workload.
2) GPU resident footprint variance across 1 hour drops by >= 35% (measured as coefficient of variation).
3) No increase in median generation latency for small batches (<4) across compatibility models.
4) E2E integration tests for graceful fallback (model variant routing) pass in staging.
5) Observability: new metrics (hot-residency-rate, drain-throughput, compaction-time) emitted and charted in Console runtime dashboard.
implementation_plan:
Phase 1 (prototype):
- Implement a Hot/Cold classifier that tags KV entries by short-term access frequency and recent token affinity within sliding windows aligned to batching epochs.
- Provide per-slab 'resilience' score: combines age, access-rate, and fragmentation density.
- Expose a coordinator API to candidate entries for micro-drain (async host writeback) and prefetch hints.

Phase 2 (integration):
- Wire classifier into the batching runtime so prefetch/drain decisions are aligned with predicted batch compositions and token affinity.
- Add cooperative micro-compaction: reclaim contiguous free blocks within a slab opportunistically between batch flushes.
- Implement a drain scheduler that respects SLO budget and can throttle writeback when tail latency approaches threshold.

Phase 3 (hardening):
- Add safety nets: immediate pinning for pinned sessions (enterprise customers), and a fast-fallback path to smaller in-memory model variants.
- Add observability and automated alerts for anomalous drain/backpressure loops.

Phase 4 (release):
- Ramp in dedicated capacity; monitor regressions; rollout to hosted API via gradual percentage-based rollout policy.
tech_design_notes:
Key algorithms and trade-offs considered: 
- Hot/Cold classifier: lightweight exponential decay counters per token-key vs. sampling-based LRU approximation. We picked a hybrid: epochal counters (low overhead) + occasional stratified sampling to detect sudden spikes.
- Drain vs. Evict: drain (async host writeback) is preferred when downstream prefetch latency is bounded and space reclamation can be amortized across micro-batches. Full eviction is used only when reclaim is urgent.
- Micro-compaction window: bounded to not block KV lookups. We schedule compaction tasks on the host-side thread pool; compaction proceeds by relocating live entries into coalesced slabs and then updating slab headers with atomic CAS. This reduces fragmentation without global stop-the-world.
- Prefetch hints: generated from recent batch token trajectories (token affinity). Prefetch ahead of predicted next-token batches with a conservative safety margin (default 2 micro-batches) to avoid useless pulls.
- I/O model: use pinned async DMA to host pinned-NVMe staging and leverage PCIe peer-to-peer where available.
- Backpressure policy: if drain throughput falls below predicted refill rate, runtime elects to reduce batch sizes preferentially for non-latency-critical routes to protect production SLOs.
experiments_and_findings:
Test harness: synthetic hotspot generator that switches hotset every 30s; mixed-size continuous batching driver (1-32 tokens).
Initial prototype results (dev cluster: A100x8, 2TB NVMe):
- Baseline (no bridge): 95th token-latency = 132ms, resident-footprint-CV = 0.48.
- Prototype (classifier + scheduled drain): 95th token-latency = 102ms (22.7% improvement), resident-footprint-CV = 0.29.
- Cost: average additional host IO of 12MB/s per GPU under heavy churn.
- Regression note: for pathological micro-burst with <10ms hotset flip, prefetch hysteresis prevented benefits; added shorter epoch sampling reduced miss rate by 8% but increased CPU cycles.

risks_and_mitigations:
Risk 1: Increased CPU utilization for classifier and compaction threads could starve serving loop. Mitigation: cap classifier sampling rate and run compaction on host worker pool with QoS.
Risk 2: Excessive host IO on NVMe may increase costs for Dedicated customers. Mitigation: expose throttle knob and autoscale drain aggressiveness.
Risk 3: Atomic slab header updates might race with concurrent lookups on older runtime microcode. Mitigation: maintain dual-version header and a short quiesce window; compatibility flag for older nodes.
Risk 4: Incorrect prefetch heuristics cause wasted host-to-GPU transfers. Mitigation: conservative prefetch budget, and falling back to LRU-only policy if detection of oscillating miss rates occurs.
